content: 1. In the study by Millard, Bailey, and Hanson (1991), the selection process for attending a maternity waiting home (MWH) was open to all women. Women considered high-risk and living at a distance were actively encouraged to reside in the MWH during the last two weeks of pregnancy. 2. In the study by Gaym, Pearson, and Soe (2012), the selection processes were not described. 3. Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra (1994) did not randomize the two groups, which means that variables (both known and unknown) were not balanced. However, efforts were made to control for important confounders, but only during the analysis stage. 4. Two studies (Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra, 1994; Gaym, Pearson, and Soe, 2012) did not specify eligibility criteria. In contrast, Millard, Bailey, and Hanson (1991) allowed all women to attend, with high-risk women encouraged to stay in the MWH. 5. All studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, with most (except Gaym, Pearson, and Soe, 2012) reporting that the settings were remote or rural. 6. The components of the MWHs varied significantly across and within studies in terms of size, location, facilities, length of stay before delivery, food provision, and additional services such as antenatal care (ANC), health education, and reduced fees for instrumental deliveries and cesarean sections. 7. All studies compared MWHs with standard care prior to facility admission. 8. All studies consistently reported a reduction in stillbirth rates following the intervention. 9. Perinatal mortality rates were lower among women who used MWHs compared to those who received standard care. 10. All studies were observational and of weak methodological quality, with a high risk of bias due to unclear methods. 11. Data collection methods appeared reliable in two studies (Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra, 1994; Larsen and Muller, 1978) as they used hospital records, but no information on validity was provided. 12. In two studies (Millard, Bailey, and Hanson, 1991; Tumwine and Dungare, 1996), the methods were not described. 13. Recruitment and selection of participants were not fully described in all studies. For example, Tumwine and Dungare (1996) relied on health center staff or trained traditional birth attendants (TBAs) to prompt women to attend MWHs. Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra (1994) recruited high-risk women, while Millard, Bailey, and Hanson (1991) allowed any woman to attend. 14. Blinding of outcome assessors and participants was unclear in all studies. 15. In Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra (1994), although the groups were not randomized, efforts were made to control for confounders during the analysis stage. 16. Two studies (Chandramohan, Cutts, and Chandra, 1994; Tumwine and Dungare, 1996) included only high-risk women, although the definition of high-risk varied between studies. 17. The components of the MWHs varied greatly in size, location, facilities, length of stay, food provision, and additional services provided. 18. All studies reported lower neonatal mortality rates when women were admitted to hospitals via MWHs. 19. One cluster randomized trial of moderate quality reported fewer maternal deaths among women exposed to a multifaceted intervention that included a small community-organized emergency transport component. However, it was not possible to attribute improvements to any single component of the intervention. 20. One cluster randomized trial of moderate quality reported significantly lower stillbirth rates among women exposed to the multifaceted intervention, but improvements could not be attributed to any single component. 21. One cluster randomized trial of moderate quality reported significantly lower perinatal mortality rates among women exposed to the intervention, but the improvements could not be attributed to any single component. 22. One cluster randomized trial of moderate quality reported significantly lower neonatal mortality rates in intervention clusters, but a quarter of target villages remained uncovered by the intervention. Improvements could not be attributed to any single component. 23. Community-organized transport schemes were evaluated in two case-control studies of weak methodological quality. These studies reported inconsistent findings, with one study showing an increase in facility births and the other showing a decrease in home births. 24. The evidence for community-organized transport schemes was of very low quality due to serious risks of bias, indirectness, and inconsistency. 25. The role of traditional birth attendants (TBAs) within the formal health system was evaluated in two studies. Both studies reported weak methodological quality, with unclear methods, unreliable data collection, and likely selection bias. 26. Data for maternal and newborn health outcomes were often self-reported in household surveys, which may have introduced reporting bias. Additionally, methods used in verbal/social autopsies may have resulted in misclassification of outcomes such as stillbirths and neonatal deaths. 27. The intervention packages evaluated were often complex and multifaceted, making it difficult to attribute improvements to any single component. Lady health workers (LHWs) played a key role in implementing these interventions.
